clue.text: As reported, wouldn't keep a rodent

indicators.note: a report is something spoken, so the phrase that follows is heard rather than read

parts.note: someone who wouldn't keep a thing would chuck it

explanation.surface: Word has it that somebody refused to have a rat or hamster as a pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As reported' tells you to say the idea out loud: a person who wouldn't keep something 'would chuck' it, and that is how the North American groundhog's other name is pronounced.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an example: the groundhog, a burrowing North American marmot, belongs to the gnawing order of mammals.

clue.text: One delivering a speech that's partly exploratory

indicators.note: only a part of the long word is wanted, a stretch of its letters in a row

explanation.surface: A speaker gives a talk that is, in places, tentative and probing.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a public speaker, especially a skilled one, is called this.

clue.text: Get rid of the tel. Editor? Some would appear upset!

indicators.note: in a down clue something upset is overturned, so the letters run from the bottom up
only some of the letters of the phrase show up, a consecutive stretch of them

explanation.surface: A call to sack the telephone desk's editor, which would annoy a few people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some would appear' picks ETELED out of 'the tel. Editor', running across the full stop, and 'upset' turns that stretch upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to erase or strike out text is to remove it, the very thing an editor does.

clue.text: Soldier in a rush, running over sand — and falling

indicators.note: the jumbled phrase goes over, that is around, the leftover letter
running suggests letters in motion, taking up new positions
the word and falls away from sand, leaving only what remains

explanation.surface: A trooper hurries across a beach and takes a tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' rearranges A RUSH into HUSAR, and 'over' wraps it around the S that is left when 'and' drops out of 'sand' ('falling').
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a light cavalryman, originally Hungarian, is one kind of military man.

clue.text: Hotchpotch display in education institute having a misprint

indicators.note: a misprint is one wrong letter printed in place of the right one

parts.note: a college is a place of further or higher education
taken as written: it is the letter wrongly printed

explanation.surface: A jumbled exhibition at a school, with an error in the printed programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having a misprint' means one letter of COLLEGE is printed wrongly as A: the first E gives way to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an artwork of assorted scraps pasted together is a jumble put on show.

clue.text: Ruddy collector standing at the roadside

definitions.text: Ruddy collector standing at the roadside

parts.words: Ruddy collector standing at the roadside
parts.note: British street mailboxes are bright red cylinders on the pavement, and letters are collected from them; ruddy is literal here, not a mild swear word

explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: in Britain the red cylinder on the pavement gathers posted mail for the postman.

clue.text: Spooner's comprehensive champ in this sort of contest

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of two words

parts.note: comprehensive means full, complete
to champ is to bite or chew noisily

explanation.surface: The clergyman's all-round title-holder takes part in a certain kind of competition.
explanation.walkthrough: FULL BITE, with the opening sounds exchanged as 'Spooner's' asks, is heard as the Spanish arena spectacle. 'Champ' is the verb to chew, not a champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Spanish spectacle of matador against toro is a kind of combat event.

clue.text: Mathematicians greet some in a peculiar fashion

indicators.note: done in a peculiar fashion, the letters are set out in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Number experts say hello to a few people rather oddly.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: specialists in shapes, lines and angles are one branch of the profession.

clue.text: Little mo

definitions.meaning: tiny, when the word is stressed on its second syllable
mo is short for moment, loosely sixty seconds

explanation.definitionFit: One spelling serves as an adjective meaning tiny and as a noun for a short stretch of time.

clue.text: Hell as spy gets tortured, unfortunately

indicators.note: something tortured is twisted out of shape, so the letters are wrenched into a new order

explanation.surface: A secret agent is put through agony on the rack, sad to say.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an adverb meaning unluckily, without good fortune.

clue.text: Race is a hit — look to join in

indicators.note: the second piece joins in, taking a place within the first

parts.note: to slam something is to hit it hard
lo is an old exclamation meaning look

explanation.surface: A sporting event proves popular, so watch for a chance to take part.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface 'a hit' is a popular success; in the wordplay it is a hard blow, which 'to join in' opens up for the old exclamation meaning look.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a zigzag ski descent between poles is one kind of timed contest.

clue.text: Description left by a couple of blokes …

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
Ray is a man's name, the first of the two
Al is a man's name, the second of the two

explanation.surface: Two chaps have written an account and left it behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is the nautical side, not the verb, and the two blokes are simply men's names, Ray and Al.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a depiction of someone in words or pictures.

clue.text: … Or by this person (in dire strait)

indicators.note: dire means dreadful, so the word beside it is in a bad state and its letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Or the account could come from this individual, who is in desperate trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots carry on from the previous clue: a description can also be made by a painter. 'Dire' rearranges STRAIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a painter is somebody who depicts a subject, which the linked previous clue describes.

clue.text: It's a crime, disturbing the peace for a while

indicators.note: to disturb things is to move them out of place, so the letters change position

explanation.surface: Breaking the quiet, even briefly, is an offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbing' rearranges IT'S A CRIME. The surface runs 'disturbing the peace' together; the definition is only the last words.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a truce, an agreed halt to fighting that may be temporary.

clue.text: Son looked after by mum — too much so, it seems!

parts.note: S is the genealogical abbreviation for son
to mother someone is to care for them as a mum does

explanation.surface: A boy is so coddled by his mum that it looks excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the whole clue: a son cared for by mum to excess is stifled.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to be stifled by excessive affection is to be cared for to a suffocating degree.

clue.text: Soldier near ridge getting shot

indicators.note: something shot is blown apart, scattering the letters

explanation.surface: An infantryman is hit by a bullet close to a hilltop.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a member of the Guards regiment, originally a bomb thrower, is a military man.

clue.text: Margaret's artificial limb

definitions.meaning: a pet form of the name Margaret; the apostrophe-s reads as 'is'
the old word for a wooden leg

explanation.definitionFit: The short form of a woman's name is also the word for a wooden leg.

clue.text: Seat in gym that's weak

parts.note: PE, physical education, is the school lesson held in the gym
W is the abbreviation for weak, used in physics for the weak force

explanation.surface: A bench in the fitness room that looks flimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the long wooden bench in a church is something to sit on.

clue.text: Dramatist being carefree (once!)

definitions.meaning: John, the 18th-century author of The Beggar's Opera
the old sense of the word, merry and light-hearted, before its modern meaning took over

explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the playwright who wrote The Beggar's Opera is also an old adjective for merry.

clue.text: Deep regret about detective dying on TV

parts.note: re means about, concerning
Inspector Morse, the Oxford detective of the British TV series, died in its final episode

explanation.surface: Viewers feel real sorrow over a sleuth's death on screen.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is the Oxford detective of a long-running British TV drama, who died in the last episode.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a painful sense of guilt and sorrow over something done.

clue.text: Answer: 'not that lady'? Possibly!

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer, as in Q and A
taken as written
her is the pronoun for that lady

explanation.surface: Asked whether it was that woman, someone replies that perhaps it wasn't.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue hints at the meaning: if the reply is 'not that lady', it may be a different one.
explanation.definitionFit: Whole-clue hint: if it is not that woman, then perhaps it is a different one.

clue.text: Odd characters with worry sneering

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters of the next word are taken: first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: Strange people, full of anxiety, curl their lips in contempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: mocking, with a twisted, sardonic expression.

clue.text: A career for a career's sake?

definitions.text: A career for a career's sake?

parts.words: A career for a career's sake?
parts.note: career means both a working life and a headlong rush: the phrase describes the frantic competitive scramble for advancement at work

explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: the competitive scramble of working life is a headlong dash made for the sake of a job.

clue.text: Plan camping?

definitions.meaning: split two and four, the letters say where a camper is, under canvas

explanation.definitionFit: A noun meaning purpose which, split in two, whimsically says where somebody under canvas is.

clue.text: Fan issues demand for instant success

definitions.meaning: to fan grain is to blow the chaff from it
split three and three, the letters are an order to triumph immediately

explanation.definitionFit: A verb for blowing chaff from grain which, split in two, reads as an order to triumph immediately.

clue.text: However, tragic king won't need a servant

parts.note: but means however

indicators.note: what the king won't need is left out of his name

parts.note: King Lear is the monarch of Shakespeare's tragedy
taken as written: the letter left out

explanation.surface: Nevertheless, a doomed monarch has no call for a manservant.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' before 'servant' is not part of the definition: it is the letter that 'won't need' removes from the name of Shakespeare's doomed monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the chief manservant of a household.

clue.text: Frantic chaser in the hunt

indicators.note: frantic means wildly agitated, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: A desperate pursuer rides with the hounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a quest to find something, as a noun.

clue.text: Positions badly situated — time to get stuck in

indicators.note: the extra letter gets stuck in, lodged within the rest
badly says the word before it is in a poor state, its letters out of order

parts.note: T is the physics abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: The posts are poorly placed, so it is the moment to roll up your sleeves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' rearranges SITUATED into ATTIUDES, and 'to get stuck in' lodges T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: stances, whether opinions held or postures of the body.

clue.text: Cute duke with yen to be conveying a nobby country image?

parts.note: twee is British for excessively sweet or cute
Y is the abbreviation for yen, the Japanese currency

explanation.surface: A sweet-looking nobleman longs to come across as landed gentry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nobby' is British slang for upper-class; the rough woollen cloth is the uniform of the British country gentry.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: wearing the rough woollen cloth of the shooting set suggests upper-class rural life.

clue.text: Ray, loving to be different, boasting in an empty manner

indicators.note: the letters are to be made different, put into another order

explanation.surface: Ray enjoys standing out from the crowd and brags hollowly about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: idle, excessive pride and bragging about oneself.

clue.text: Small class always intelligent

parts.note: cl. is the short form of class
ever means always, as in ever faithful

explanation.surface: A school group with few pupils is invariably bright.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: quick-witted and bright.

clue.text: Reliable, in the main?

parts.note: the main is the open ocean, so this is about a vessel that can be trusted afloat rather than something mostly dependable

explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: a vessel fit to sail the ocean can be trusted on the water.
